questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y={e}^{-3x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+3(u{e}^{-3x}) & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3u{e}^{-3x}+3u{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}}+\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & ={e}^{-3x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-3x} \\  & =x{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =6\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x=\frac{{e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =6{e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\  & =6{e}^{-3x}(\frac{{e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}}{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{-3x}({e}^{3x}-{e}^{-3x}) \\  & =3-3{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =3-3{e}^{-6x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 3-3{e}^{-6x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =3x+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-6x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =3x{e}^{3x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & =16\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\ {u}^{′} & =16{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x=\frac{{e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =16{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡4x \\  & =16{e}^{-4x}(\frac{{e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}}{2}) \\  & =8{e}^{-4x}({e}^{4x}-{e}^{-4x}) \\  & =8-8{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =8-8{e}^{-8x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 8-8{e}^{-8x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =8x+{e}^{-8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =8x{e}^{4x}+{e}^{-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
u(x)e4x
u(x)e4x
u(x)e−4x
u(x)e8x
u(x)e−8x
u(x)e12x

8x+e−8x
8x+e−8x
8x+2e−8x

8xe4x+e−4x

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2y={x}^{2}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{2x})}^{′}-2(u{e}^{2x}) & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2u{e}^{2x}-2u{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}}-\cancel{2u{e}^{2x}} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{-2x}({x}^{2}) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{2x} \\  & =\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{2x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\int {e}^{-2x}({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=1-4x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+3(u{e}^{-3x}) & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3u{e}^{-3x}+3u{e}^{-3x} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}}+\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{3x}(1-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{3x}(1-4x) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-3x} \\  & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-3x} \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

5.Solving First-Order Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters?

Consider the first-order linear ODE dydx+3y=1−4x. We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form
u(x)e−3x
u(x)e−3x
u(x)e3x
u(x)e−4x
u(x)e4x
u(x)ex
.

Solving for u, we have u(x)=
∫e3x(1−4x)dx
∫e3x(1−4x)dx
∫e−3x(1−4x)dx
∫e3x(4x−1)dx
∫e3x(1+4x)dx
.

e3x∫e−3x(1−4x)dx
